16. supplementary.tex:342/main.tex:381 — "effect---the within-pool" → 逗号或分号

1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related_work}
3	
4	\paragraph{Training-free LLM IE.}
5	Training-free LLM IE spans instruction tuning \cite{instructuie-2023}, code-style schema encoding \cite{knowcoder-2024,codeie-2023}, annotation-guided extraction \cite{gollie-2024,adelie-2024}, schema-driven decoding \cite{slot-2025,oneke-2025}, and constrained JSON decoding \cite{json-schema-bench-2025}. For NER, methods include zero-shot decomposition \cite{xie-zeroshot-ner-2023,promptner-2023}, distillation \cite{uniner-2024}, and bidirectional encoders \cite{gliner-2024,gliner2-2025}. For RE, recent work examines zero-shot relation triplet extraction via prompting \cite{relationprompt-2022} and revisits relation extraction in the LLM era \cite{wadhwa-re-llm-2023}. These methods perform well with moderate schemas (4--20 types) but none investigates how performance degrades as schema complexity scales, nor proposes quantitative metrics for inter-type confusability.
6	
7	\paragraph{Schema complexity in IE.}
8	The most directly related work is LLM-PEE \cite{llm-pee-2025}, which partitions large event schemas by type embedding similarity. Our work differs in three ways: (1)~we conduct controlled analysis to understand \emph{why} extraction degrades rather than developing an engineering solution; (2)~our BCS-controlled experiments isolate count from confusability, which LLM-PEE conflates; (3)~our SDGD experiments reveal that merge amplification---not partitioning quality---is the bottleneck in decompose-then-merge pipelines. Specifically, LLM-PEE employs union merge across sub-schema extractions, which our \S\ref{sec:sdgd} analysis shows causes precision to collapse from 0.56 to 0.21 in NER as false positives accumulate across passes; RE avoids this because closed-set classification does not require span reconciliation, explaining why LLM-PEE's decomposition succeeds for relation/event tasks but faces unresolved merge challenges on span-level extraction. Other approaches address schema complexity via hard negative mining \cite{iepile-2024}, schema definition optimization \cite{parse-2025}, multi-agent debate \cite{crossagentie-2025,cmas-ner-2025}, schema-aware decomposition for event extraction \cite{dee-2024}, and active prompting \cite{reflect-learn-2026}; all treat it as an engineering problem rather than isolating the underlying degradation mechanisms. Concurrently, \citet{haystack-to-needle-2025} reduces label spaces via iterative LLM filtering, an engineering complement to our analytical approach. Our framework explains \emph{why} such reduction works: it implicitly lowers batch confusability.
9	
10	\paragraph{Schema complexity in dialogue and IE.} The Schema-Guided Dialogue dataset~\cite{rastogi2020towards} and SGD-X~\cite{lee2022sgd} document performance degradation with schema linguistic variation. \citet{li2023evaluating} observe count-dependent degradation in ChatGPT IE. \citet{volkanovska2024ner} categorize LLM NER errors including type confusion. The relationship between label similarity and classification confusion has precedent in traditional ML: hierarchical classification suffers sibling confusion proportional to inter-class proximity \citep{deng-2010-imagenet}, label confusion matrices improve text classification \citep{guo-2021-label-confusion}, and classification confusion captures semantic similarity \citep{zhou-2025-rethinking}. Hierarchical label sets reduce class confusion in zero-shot image classification \citep{novack-2023-chils}; enriched type descriptions improve zero-shot NER \citep{cocchieri-2025-zeroner}---both orthogonal to our confusability-aware batching.
11	
12	\paragraph{SCS novelty.} SCS shares its formal definition---pairwise cosine similarity of type name embeddings---with the partitioning criterion used in LLM-PEE~\cite{llm-pee-2025} for schema decomposition. Our contribution is not the metric itself but the controlled experimental framework that isolates confusability's predictive relationship with extraction degradation, distinguishing it from the engineering use in prior work. The modest pairwise effect size ($r^2 = 1.3$--$1.7\%$) is consistent with standards for individual-difference predictors in behavioral research \citep{cohen-1988-power}, where such magnitudes are considered ``small but real'' effects that compound at the aggregate level \citep{lakens-2013-effect-size}.
13	
14	\paragraph{Embedding anisotropy.}
15	Our centrality confound (\S\ref{sec:centrality_confound}) connects to representation degeneration: embeddings collapse into narrow cones \cite{gao-repr-degen-2019,ethayarajh-contextual-2019}, but local clusters can be isotropic \cite{cai-isotropy-clusters-2021}---explaining why MAVEN's single-ontology types conflate confusability with centrality.
16	
17

1	\section{Schema Decomposition: Failure, Diagnosis, and Mitigation}
2	\label{sec:sdgd}
3	
4	A natural intervention against confusability-driven degradation is to partition the schema so that confusable types never co-occur in the same prompt. We test this idea with \textbf{Schema-DAG-Guided Decomposition} (SDGD\footnote{SDGD (Schema Decomposition and Grouping for Degradation mitigation) is an adopted abbreviation for schema decomposition and grouping; the graph structure is undirected.}), which uses greedy graph coloring on the pairwise SCS graph to assign types to low-confusability batches.
5	
6	We construct a thresholded confusability graph $G = (V, E)$ where each type is a vertex and an edge connects types $t_i, t_j$ whenever $\text{SCS}(t_i, t_j) > \tau$. Greedy graph coloring (\textsc{largest\_first}) assigns each type to a color such that no two adjacent---i.e., highly confusable---types share a batch. Each color class forms one extraction batch. For NER, predictions from all batches are merged via set union; for RE, each instance is routed to the batch containing its gold type (oracle routing). We test four NER modes: (i)~\textbf{single\_pass}, the undecomposed baseline; (ii)~\textbf{sdgd\_zero}, SCS-guided partitioning; (iii)~\textbf{random\_batch}, random partitioning with matched batch sizes; and (iv)~\textbf{per\_type}, each type extracted in isolation. Every mode falls below the single-pass NER baseline: SDGD obtains F1\,=\,0.251, random batching 0.320, per-type 0.292, versus 0.445 for single-pass (Table~\ref{tab:sdgd_results}, Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_sdgd}).
7	
8	\paragraph{Merge amplification in NER.}
9	The core failure mechanism is \emph{merge amplification}: presenting the same text to the model $k$ times with different type subsets causes each pass to independently generate entity predictions, and union merge accumulates all of them into a single output. Each pass produces an independent set of span predictions; because LLM outputs are not calibrated across passes \cite{llm-calibration-survey-2024}, the same span may receive conflicting type labels from different passes, or hallucinated entities may appear in passes where the correct type is absent. Union merge retains all predictions, so false positives scale with $k$ while true positives are bounded by the fixed set of gold entities.
10	
11	Quantitatively, single-pass precision (0.563) collapses to 0.210--0.249 after union merge across 8 batches, while recall gains are modest (0.368 $\to$ 0.314 for sdgd\_zero, 0.446 for random batch). The net F1 loss is substantial: 0.445 $\to$ 0.251 (sdgd\_zero) or 0.320 (random batch). Per-type extraction (66 batches) pushes recall to 0.586 but precision to 0.194 (F1\,=\,0.292), confirming that the precision--recall imbalance intensifies with the number of passes. Random batching outperforms confusability-aware SDGD on NER (0.320 vs.\ 0.251) because the dominant degradation source---merge amplification---is independent of batch composition; any multi-pass scheme suffers from it regardless of grouping quality.
12	
13	\paragraph{Confidence gating does not resolve merge amplification.}
14	Confidence-based gating (retaining only predictions above threshold) trades recall for precision but does not recover net F1 (0.251$\to$0.241), confirming that merge artifacts are systemic rather than confined to low-confidence predictions (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_sdgd}).
15	
16	\paragraph{Why NER fails but RE does not.}
17	Merge amplification is specific to span-level tasks. Each NER pass independently proposes entity spans, and union merge must resolve conflicting boundaries and type assignments, degrading systematically with pass count. RE avoids this mechanism entirely: under oracle routing, each relation instance receives a single classification from the batch containing its gold type, requiring no span reconciliation and eliminating the multi-pass interference that causes SDGD to fail on NER. This makes RE a clean testbed for evaluating whether confusability-aware decomposition improves accuracy once merge artifacts are removed.
18	
19	\enlargethispage*{9\baselineskip}
20	\paragraph{Oracle routing as performance ceiling.}
21	Oracle routing routes each test instance to the batch containing its gold type, eliminating cross-type confusion within each batch. On FewRel 80-relation RE, oracle-routed decomposition achieves 0.802 accuracy versus 0.504 for the single-pass baseline---a gain of +29.8\,pp (Table~\ref{tab:batch_composition}). This is the strongest positive finding of the decomposition experiments: it demonstrates that type confusability is indeed a key driver of degradation in RE, and that performance recovers substantially when confusable types are separated.
22	
23	However, oracle routing requires gold labels and is not deployable. The gap between the oracle ceiling and practical routing reveals an important asymmetry: while \emph{any} decomposition benefits enormously from removing the 80-type bottleneck (+28.4\,pp for random batching, +29.8\,pp for graph coloring), the \emph{additional} benefit of confusability-aware grouping over random grouping is modest (+1.4\,pp, $p \approx 0.19$). The confusability-aware strategy ranks 13th out of 15 random seeds, limited by the narrow BCS margin (0.006) between graph-coloring and random batches at this partition granularity. Finer-grained partitioning or alternative confusability metrics may be needed to translate the oracle-demonstrated potential into significant practical gains.
24	
25	\paragraph{Practical routing strategies.}
26	We evaluate five non-oracle routing strategies on FewRel 80-relation RE using a coarser 5-group decomposition (oracle ceiling: 72.4\%, +22.0\,pp; cf.\ +29.8\,pp under 17-group decomposition in Table~\ref{tab:batch_composition}): max-confidence (all predictions), max-confidence (positive only), none-aware selection, margin-based routing, and random assignment. All five perform below the single-pass baseline (50.4\%), with the best practical strategy reaching only 36.5\% accuracy (Table~\ref{tab:routing_strategies}, Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_routing}). The root cause is constrained decoding: the enum constraint forces the model to produce a confident type prediction for every sub-schema, even when the correct type is absent from the candidate set. As a result, 73.4\% of instances receive positive predictions from 3--5 sub-schemas simultaneously, and the none-rate per sub-schema is only 20--40\%. Because every sub-schema produces high-confidence outputs, confidence signals become unreliable and all confidence-based routing fails. Free-form generation or calibrated confidence estimation may provide more reliable routing signals for future work.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Training-free\footnote{We use ``training-free'' and ``zero-shot'' interchangeably to denote prompting without parameter updates.}\footnote{Code and data will be released upon acceptance. Anonymous review materials: \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/schema-dag-extraction}} LLM information extraction---prompting a large language model with a target schema and asking it to extract structured information without any task-specific fine-tuning---enables rapid deployment across new domains and ontologies. This zero-shot paradigm eliminates the need for labeled data, making it attractive for applications where annotation is expensive or schemas evolve frequently \cite{llm4ie-survey-2024}. Yet the paradigm carries a critical limitation: performance degrades sharply as the number of candidate types in the prompt schema grows. On named entity recognition, recall drops from 0.72 with a single candidate type to a plateau of ${\sim}$0.27 across intermediate schema sizes (22--44 types) before partial recovery at full-schema. On relation extraction, accuracy falls from 85.7\% with one relation to 49.5\% with 80 relations (sentence-level) and from 88.0\% to 38.7\% with 96 relations (document-level)---near or exceeding halving. This degradation is not academic: real-world ontologies routinely define 50--200+ types, placing them squarely in the regime where training-free extraction becomes unreliable.

What explains this degradation? Prior decomposition strategies \cite{uniner-2024,llm-pee-2025,parse-2025} conflate two mechanisms: having more types to discriminate among (count) and having semantically similar types to confuse (confusability) (hereafter Channel~1 and Channel~2). None isolates which factor predicts the gains (\S\ref{sec:related_work}).

We ask three questions. \textbf{RQ1}: Does type confusability independently predict extraction degradation beyond the effect of type count? \textbf{RQ2}: Through what mechanisms do count and confusability each degrade performance? \textbf{RQ3}: Can confusability-aware schema decomposition improve extraction quality?

To our knowledge, we present the first controlled study isolating type confusability from type count via stratified design in zero-shot LLM IE, spanning NER, RE, and event detection (ED). We operationalize confusability via the \emph{Schema Confusability Score} (SCS)---pairwise embedding cosine similarity---and its batch-level aggregation, the \emph{Batch Confusability Score} (BCS). We evaluate on Few-NERD \cite{fewnerd-2021}, FewRel \cite{fewrel-2018}, DocRED \cite{docred-2019}, and MAVEN \cite{maven-2020} using Qwen3-32B (\S\ref{sec:experimental_setup}).

Our experiments yield five findings: (1)~degradation operates through two channels---count-driven recall decline (up to $-$49\,pp at intermediate schema sizes for document-level RE) and confusability-driven type substitution (typical-batch gap ${\approx}\,2.2$\,pp; quartile $\Delta = -5.3$\,pp)---an asymmetric relationship where count dominates, consistent with bounded interaction in RE (TOST $p = 0.003$ at $\pm 3$\,pp) but coupled in NER where NER recall exhibits non-monotonic recovery at full-schema; (2)~pairwise SCS predicts type confusion ($r = 0.112$--$0.129$), the first factor empirically isolated in controlled zero-shot IE; (3)~effects are consistent across schema sizes and granularities (BCS slopes: $p = 0.60$; DocRED: slope $= -0.71$, $R^2 = 0.53$), and directionally consistent across prompt designs, with attenuated magnitude under improved prompts; (4)~per-type aggregation is confounded by centrality on homogeneous schemas; (5)~NER decomposition fails due to merge amplification; RE confusability-aware grouping yields no significant improvement over random (+1.4\,pp, $p \approx 0.19$, n.s.) despite oracle routing recovering +29.8\,pp.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Training-free\footnote{We use ``training-free'' and ``zero-shot'' interchangeably to denote prompting without parameter updates.}\footnote{Code and data will be released upon acceptance. Anonymous review materials: \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/schema-dag-extraction}} LLM information extraction (prompting a large language model with a target schema and asking it to extract structured information without any task-specific fine-tuning) enables rapid deployment across new domains and ontologies. This zero-shot paradigm eliminates the need for labeled data, making it attractive for applications where annotation is expensive or schemas evolve frequently \cite{llm4ie-survey-2024}. Yet the paradigm carries a critical limitation: performance degrades sharply as the number of candidate types in the prompt schema grows. On named entity recognition, recall drops from 0.72 with a single candidate type to a plateau of ${\sim}$0.27 across intermediate schema sizes (22--44 types) before partial recovery at full-schema. On relation extraction, accuracy falls from 85.7\% with one relation to 49.5\% with 80 relations (sentence-level) and from 88.0\% to 38.7\% with 96 relations (document-level)---near or exceeding halving. This degradation is not academic: real-world ontologies routinely define 50--200+ types, placing them squarely in the regime where training-free extraction becomes unreliable.

What explains this degradation? Prior decomposition strategies \cite{uniner-2024,llm-pee-2025,parse-2025} conflate two factors: having more types to discriminate among (count) and having semantically similar types to confuse (confusability) (hereafter Dimension~1 and Dimension~2). None isolates which factor predicts the gains (\S\ref{sec:related_work}).

This study combines correlational analyses with quasi-experimental manipulation (BCS-controlled batches) to characterize how schema properties predict extraction accuracy.

We ask three questions. \textbf{RQ1}: Does type confusability independently predict extraction degradation beyond the effect of type count? \textbf{RQ2}: Through what mechanisms do count and confusability each degrade performance? \textbf{RQ3}: Can confusability-aware schema decomposition improve extraction quality?

To our knowledge, we present the first controlled study isolating type confusability from type count via stratified design in zero-shot LLM IE, spanning NER, RE, and event detection (ED). We operationalize confusability via the \emph{Schema Confusability Score} (SCS), defined as pairwise embedding cosine similarity, and its batch-level aggregation, the \emph{Batch Confusability Score} (BCS). We evaluate on Few-NERD \cite{fewnerd-2021}, FewRel \cite{fewrel-2018}, DocRED \cite{docred-2019}, and MAVEN \cite{maven-2020} using Qwen3-32B (\S\ref{sec:experimental_setup}).

Our experiments yield five findings: (1)~degradation operates through two channels---count-driven recall decline (up to $-$49\,pp at intermediate schema sizes for document-level RE) and confusability-driven type substitution (typical-batch gap ${\approx}\,2.2$\,pp; quartile $\Delta = -5.3$\,pp)---an asymmetric relationship where count dominates, consistent with bounded interaction in RE (TOST $p = 0.003$ at $\pm 3$\,pp) but coupled in NER where NER recall exhibits non-monotonic recovery at full-schema; (2)~pairwise SCS predicts type confusion ($r = 0.112$--$0.129$), the first factor empirically isolated in controlled zero-shot IE; (3)~effects are consistent across schema sizes and granularities (BCS slopes: $p = 0.60$; DocRED: slope $= -0.71$, $R^2 = 0.53$), and directionally consistent across prompt designs, with attenuated magnitude under improved prompts; (4)~per-type aggregation is confounded by centrality on homogeneous schemas; (5)~NER decomposition fails due to merge amplification; RE confusability-aware grouping yields no significant improvement over random (+1.4\,pp, $p \approx 0.19$, n.s.) despite oracle routing recovering +29.8\,pp.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=2pt]
    \item \textbf{Count dominates confusability by ${\sim}20\times$ in typical batches.} Through stratified design isolating count from confusability, we show count effects ($-$42\% to $-$56\% recall) dwarf typical confusability effects (2.2\,pp), counter to decomposition literature's implicit assumption that confusability is the primary bottleneck. Interaction is bounded (TOST $p = 0.003$ at $\pm 3$\,pp) in RE but not in NER, where boundary and type ambiguity couple (\S\ref{sec:multi_channel}).
\item \textbf{Pairwise embedding similarity predicts type confusion.} SCS correlates with confusion rates ($r = 0.112$--$0.129$), with centrality confound identified on homogeneous schemas---invalidating naive per-type aggregation (\S\ref{sec:scs-validation}).
\item \textbf{BCS generalizes across tasks.} BCS--accuracy slopes are consistent across schema sizes ($p = 0.60$) and replicate at document level (DocRED: $R^2 = 0.22\text{--}0.53$) (\S\ref{sec:bcs_controlled}).
\item \textbf{Schema decomposition exposes systematic routing failure.} Naive merge strategies (union, confidence-gated) collapse NER precision from 0.56 to 0.21. On RE, we evaluate seven routing strategies (oracle, five practical heuristics, random); all practical strategies fall below the single-pass baseline (best 36.5\% vs.\ 50.4\%), because constrained decoding eliminates reliable sub-schema confidence signals. Oracle routing recovers +29.8\,pp, but confusability-aware grouping adds only +1.4\,pp ($p \approx 0.19$) over random, leaving deployable routing as an open challenge (\S\ref{sec:sdgd}).
\end{enumerate}

On named entity recognition, recall drops from 0.72 with a single candidate type to a plateau of ${\sim}$0.27 across intermediate schema sizes (22--44 types) before partial recovery at full-schema. On relation extraction, accuracy falls from 85.7\% with one relation to 49.5\% with 80 relations (sentence-level) and from 88.0\% to 38.7\% with 96 relations (document-level)---near or exceeding halving. This degradation is not academic: real-world ontologies routinely define 50--200+ types, placing them squarely in the regime where training-free extraction becomes unreliable.

What explains this degradation? Prior decomposition strategies \cite{uniner-2024,llm-pee-2025,parse-2025} conflate two factors: having more types to discriminate among (count) and having semantically similar types to confuse (confusability) (hereafter Dimension~1 and Dimension~2). For RE, recent work examines zero-shot relation triplet extraction via prompting \cite{relationprompt-2022} and revisits relation extraction in the LLM era \cite{wadhwa-re-llm-2023}. These methods perform well with moderate schemas (4--20 types) but none investigates how performance degrades as schema complexity scales, nor proposes quantitative metrics for inter-type confusability.
\paragraph{Schema complexity in IE.}

-The most directly related work is LLM-PEE \cite{llm-pee-2025}, which partitions large event schemas by type embedding similarity. Our work differs in three ways: (1)~we conduct controlled analysis to understand \emph{why} extraction degrades rather than developing an engineering solution; (2)~our BCS-controlled experiments isolate count from confusability, which LLM-PEE conflates; (3)~our SDGD experiments reveal that merge amplification---not partitioning quality---is the bottleneck in decompose-then-merge pipelines. \label{sec:sdgd}

-A natural intervention against confusability-driven degradation is to partition the schema so that confusable types never co-occur in the same prompt. We test this idea with \textbf{Schema-DAG-Guided Decomposition} (SDGD\footnote{SDGD (Schema Decomposition and Grouping for Degradation mitigation) is an adopted abbreviation for schema decomposition and grouping; the graph structure is undirected.}), which uses greedy graph coloring on the pairwise SCS graph to assign types to low-confusability batches.

We construct a thresholded confusability graph $G = (V, E)$ where each type is a vertex and an edge connects types $t_i, t_j$ whenever $\text{SCS}(t_i, t_j) > \tau$. Greedy graph coloring (\textsc{largest\_first}) assigns each type to a color such that no two adjacent---i.e., highly confusable---types share a batch. Each color class forms one extraction batch. For NER, predictions from all batches are merged via set union; for RE, each instance is routed to the batch containing its gold type (oracle routing). We test four NER modes: (i)~\textbf{single\_pass}, the undecomposed baseline; (ii)~\textbf{sdgd\_zero}, SCS-guided partitioning; (iii)~\textbf{random\_batch}, random partitioning with matched batch sizes; and (iv)~\textbf{per\_type}, each type extracted in isolation. Every mode falls below the single-pass NER baseline: SDGD obtains F1\,=\,0.251, random batching 0.320, per-type 0.292, versus 0.445 for single-pass (Table~\ref{tab:sdgd_results}, Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_sdgd}).

\paragraph{Merge amplification in NER.}

The core failure mechanism is \emph{merge amplification}: presenting the same text to the model $k$ times with different type subsets causes each pass to independently generate entity predictions, and union merge accumulates all of them into a single output. Each pass produces an independent set of span predictions; because LLM outputs are not calibrated across passes \cite{llm-calibration-survey-2024}, the same span may receive conflicting type labels from different passes, or hallucinated entities may appear in passes where the correct type is absent. Union merge retains all predictions, so false positives scale with $k$ while true positives are bounded by the fixed set of gold entities.
